newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bonos jump on rate cut, but best is yet to come.
newsitem.headline: Bonos jump on rate cut, but best is yet to come.

text.p: A surprise official rate cut on Thursday fueled Spain's debt market, underscoring rising hopes that short-term rates would soon be slashed down to the levels of Spain's other European Union partners preparing to launch the planned single currency.
The market whittled away diligently at longer-term yields in 1996, convinced that Spain would get into shape for the euro's launch.
Now the market is concentrating on the short end for the start of economic and monetary union.

"If Spain enters EMU from the start the spread between official rates (Spain and Germany's) has to decline from the current 300 basis points to zero," said Alfredo Urrutia chief economist at Societe General in Madrid.
Germany's key money market rate, the "repo", is currently at three percent. Spain's equivalent is at six percent, down from nine percent at the start of last year.

"We can't expect to have the same rate as Germany at the end of this year, but it has to be there at a certain point before January 1999, when they'll fix the currency parities," said Valentine Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais.
Spain's short-end rates declined sharply in recent weeks as the market began to price in deep cuts by the central bank.
"The two-year note has already discounted an official key money market rate of around five percent by June, and at 4.75 percent by September," said Urrutia.
On Wednesday, yields set a record low of 5.342 percent from 5.865 percent on January 2, at the Treasury's six-month bill auction.
"I do not know how many times they'll cut in 1997, but for sure this is only the first one," said Luca Jellinek, analyst at Paribas Capital Market in London.
While the 10-year spread over Bunds was trading today at around 90 basis points, the three-year differential was around 180 basis points and the two-year at 200 bps.
Dealers, after having gnawed the 10-year spread from 330 bps in March 1996 to around 100 at the end of December, said the meat left for this year was now in the shorter-end.
"I'm not saying that this year we'll have another party like 1996, but people are still holding Spain where there is still more upward potential," said Urrutia.
And economists say the value is in two and three year bonds now.
"The levels of the two and three year spreads seem too high to me, so I really expect they can go lower quickly," said Fernandez, adding he is suggesting buying along this part of the yield curve.
Buying in the short end of the yield curve and the expectation of further reductions in the official rate were supporting the peseta, which was slightly stronger against the mark.
At 1345 GMT it was trading at around 83.54/56 versus the mark, having closed yesterday around 83.65/67.
Further interest rate reductions could be delivered to the market as soon as next month, analysts added.
"Another 25 basis point cut to 5.75 percent may be approved right after the January CPI, around mid February," Urrutia said.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
